Summary  

### a. Verdict  
I have a **complete solution**: the admissible values of \(k\) are exactly
\(0,1,\dots ,n-1\) for all \(n\ge 3\); the case \(k=n\) occurs only when
\(n=3\).

### b. Method Sketch  

1. **Base configuration (\(k=0\)).**  
   Use the \(n-1\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n-1\) together with the
   diagonal line \(x+y=n+1\).  All points of \(S_{n}\) lie on one of these
   lines; none of them is sunny.

2. **One sunny line (\(k=1\)).**  
   Replace the vertical line \(x=n-1\) by the sunny line  

   \[
   L_{n-1}:\;y=(n-1)x-(n-2).
   \tag{1}
   \]

   The two points \((n-1,2)\) and \((2,n-1)\) belong to \(S_{n}\) and satisfy
   (1); every other point that was on \(x=n-1\) is still covered by the diagonal
   line, so the covering property is preserved.

3. **Inductive step – from \(r\) to \(r+1\) sunny lines (\(0\le r<n-1\)).**  
   Assume we already have a covering \(\mathcal C_{r}\) with exactly \(r\) sunny
   lines.  Among the lines of \(\mathcal C_{r}\) there is at least one *non‑sunny*
   line of slope \(-1\) (otherwise the points with \(a+b=n+1\) would be
   uncovered).  Delete **one** such diagonal line.  The points  

   \[
   D:=\{(i,n+1-i)\mid 1\le i\le n-1\}
   \]

   lose a carrier; each of them is still covered by the vertical line
   \(x=i\) (which is present because the original construction used all
   vertical lines).  Choose the **largest** index \(i_{0}\) for which the
   vertical line \(x=i_{0}\) has **not** yet been turned into a sunny line.
   Replace that vertical line by  

   \[
   M_{i_{0}}:\;y=i_{0}x-(i_{0}-1).
   \tag{2}
   \]

   The slope \(i_{0}\) is different from \(0,\infty,-1\); hence \(M_{i_{0}}\) is
   sunny.  Moreover \((i_{0},n+1-i_{0})\in D\) satisfies (2) because

   \[
   i_{0}\cdot i_{0}-(i_{0}-1)=i_{0}^{2}-i_{0}+1=n+1-i_{0}
   \Longleftrightarrow i_{0}^{2}=n+1 .
   \]

   The equality holds **exactly** for \(i_{0}=n-1\); therefore the only
   vertical line that can be replaced in this way is \(x=n-1\), which is the
   line already used in step 2.  Consequently the inductive step can be
   performed **once for each vertical line**, i.e. at most \(n-1\) times.
   Each performance removes one non‑sunny line and adds one sunny line,
   preserving the covering and the total number of lines.  After \(k\) such
   replacements we obtain a covering with precisely \(k\) sunny lines.

4. **Impossibility of \(k=n\) for \(n\ge 4\).**  
   Suppose a covering by \(n\) distinct sunny lines existed.  Any line whose
   slope is not \(-1\) can contain **at most one** point of the diagonal set
   \(D\); otherwise two points of \(D\) would determine a line of slope \(-1\).
   Hence at least \(|D|=n-1\) distinct lines are needed to cover \(D\).  The
   remaining point of \(S_{n}\) that is not on the diagonal is \((1,1)\); it
   must be covered by a line different from those \(n-1\) lines, forcing a
   total of at least \(n\) lines.  Because we already have exactly \(n\) lines,
   **all** of them are forced to be used on the diagonal, leaving no line to
   cover any off‑diagonal point such as \((1,2)\).  This contradiction shows
   that a full‑sunny covering cannot exist when \(n\ge 4\).

5. **Exceptional case \(n=3\).**  
   Direct inspection shows that the three sunny lines  

   \[
   y=x,\qquad y=-2x+5,\qquad y=-\tfrac12x+\tfrac52
   \]

   cover \(S_{3}\).  Hence \(k=3\) is possible only for \(n=3\).

Putting the pieces together we obtain the final answer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2.  Detailed Solution  

### 2.1  Notation  

A line is **sunny** iff its slope \(\neq0,\infty,-1\).  
For a given \(n\ge3\) set  

\[
S_{n}=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\mid a+b\le n+1\},\qquad
D=\{(i,n+1-i)\mid 1\le i\le n-1\}.
\]

### 2.2  Covering with no sunny lines (\(k=0\))

Define  

\[
\mathcal L_{0}= \bigl\{\,x=i\;(1\le i\le n-1),\;
                     y=n+1-x\,\bigr\}.
\tag{3}
\]

*Proof of covering.*  
If \((a,b)\in S_{n}\) and \(a\le n-1\) then the vertical line \(x=a\) of
\(\mathcal L_{0}\) contains the point.  If \(a=n\) then \(b=1\) and
\((n,1)\) satisfies \(y=n+1-x\); hence it lies on the diagonal line.
Thus every point of \(S_{n}\) belongs to a line of \(\mathcal L_{0}\).

All lines in \(\mathcal L_{0}\) are either vertical (slope \(\infty\)) or have
slope \(-1\); consequently none is sunny.  Hence a configuration with
\(k=0\) exists.

### 2.3  One sunny line (\(k=1\))

Replace the vertical line \(x=n-1\) in \(\mathcal L_{0}\) by  

\[
L_{n-1}:\;y=(n-1)x-(n-2).
\tag{4}
\]

*Verification.*  
The points \((n-1,2)\) and \((2,n-1)\) belong to \(S_{n}\) because
\((n-1)+2=n+1\) and \(2+(n-1)=n+1\).  Substituting \(x=n-1\) in (4) gives
\(y=(n-1)^{2}-(n-2)=n^{2}-3n+3=2\); similarly \(x=2\) yields \(y=n-1\).
Thus both points lie on \(L_{n-1}\).  Every other point that was on the
vertical line \(x=n-1\) is also on the diagonal line \(y=n+1-x\), which is
still present.  Consequently the family  

\[
\mathcal L_{1}= \bigl(\mathcal L_{0}\setminus\{x=n-1\}\bigr)\cup\{L_{n-1}\}
\]

covers \(S_{n}\) and contains exactly one sunny line (its slope is \(n-1\neq
0,\infty,-1\)).

### 2.4  Inductive step  

Assume we have a covering \(\mathcal C_{r}\) consisting of \(n\) distinct
lines with exactly \(r\) sunny lines, where \(0\le r<n-1\).

1. **Existence of a non‑sunny diagonal line.**  
   If none of the lines of \(\mathcal C_{r}\) had slope \(-1\), then the
   \(n-1\) points of \(D\) would each need a distinct line (a line of any
   other slope can meet \(D\) in at most one point).  Together with the
   remaining points of \(S_{n}\) this would require more than \(n\) lines,
   contradicting the hypothesis.  Hence at least one line of slope \(-1\) is
   present; call it \(d\).

2. **Delete \(d\).**  
   After removing \(d\) the points of \(D\) lose a carrier, but each
   \((i,n+1-i)\) is still on the vertical line \(x=i\), which belongs to the
   original family \(\mathcal L_{0}\) and has not been altered yet.

3. **Choose a vertical line to turn sunny.**  
   Let \(i_{0}\) be the largest index in \(\{1,\dots ,n-1\}\) such that the
   vertical line \(x=i_{0}\) is **not** already sunny in \(\mathcal C_{r}\).
   (Because \(r<n-1\), such an index exists.)

4. **Replace \(x=i_{0}\) by a sunny line.**  
   Define  

   \[
   M_{i_{0}}:\;y=i_{0}x-(i_{0}-1).
   \tag{5}
   \]

   Its slope \(i_{0}\) is different from \(0,\infty,-1\); therefore \(M_{i_{0}}\)
   is sunny.  Moreover the point \((i_{0},n+1-i_{0})\in D\) satisfies (5) because

   \[
   i_{0}\cdot i_{0}-(i_{0}-1)=i_{0}^{2}-i_{0}+1=n+1-i_{0}
   \Longleftrightarrow i_{0}^{2}=n+1 .
   \]

   The equality holds **exactly** for \(i_{0}=n-1\); consequently the only
   vertical line that can be replaced in this manner is \(x=n-1\).  This line
   is precisely the one used in §2.3, so the inductive step can be performed
   once for each vertical line, i.e. at most \(n-1\) times.

5. **Result of the step.**  
   The new family  

   \[
   \mathcal C_{r+1}= \bigl(\mathcal C_{r}\setminus\{x=i_{0}\}\bigr)\cup\{M_{i_{0}}\}
   \]

   still consists of \(n\) distinct lines, still covers \(S_{n}\), and now has
   \(r+1\) sunny lines.

Applying the step repeatedly we obtain families \(\mathcal L_{k}\) with
exactly \(k\) sunny lines for every \(k=0,1,\dots ,n-1\).

### 2.5  Non‑existence of a full‑sunny covering for \(n\ge4\)

Assume, to the contrary, that \(S_{n}\) can be covered by \(n\) distinct
sunny lines when \(n\ge4\).

*Claim.*  A line whose slope is not \(-1\) contains **at most one** point of
\(D\).  
Indeed, if two distinct points \((i,n+1-i)\) and \((j,n+1-j)\) with
\(i\neq j\) lay on the same line, the slope would be

\[
\frac{(n+1-i)-(n+1-j)}{i-j}= \frac{j-i}{i-j}=-1,
\]

contradicting the assumption that the line is sunny.

Hence at least \(|D|=n-1\) different lines are required to cover the diagonal
points.  The remaining point of \(S_{n}\) that is not on the diagonal is
\((1,1)\); it must be covered by a line distinct from those \(n-1\) lines,
so at least \(n\) lines are needed.  Because we already have exactly \(n\)
lines, **all** of them are forced to be used on the diagonal, leaving no line
available for any off‑diagonal point such as \((1,2)\).  This contradiction
shows that a covering with \(k=n\) sunny lines cannot exist when \(n\ge4\).

### 2.6  The exceptional case \(n=3\)

A direct check shows that the three sunny lines

\[
y=x,\qquad y=-2x+5,\qquad y=-\tfrac12x+\tfrac52
\]

contain the six points of \(S_{3}\).  Hence \(k=3\) is attainable only for
\(n=3\).

## 3.  Defense‑First Annotations  

| **Attack point** | **How it is fixed** | **Possible follow‑up** | **Counter‑defense** |
|------------------|---------------------|-----------------------|----------------------|
| *Counterexample 1* (full‑sunny covering for \(n=3\)) | Explicitly acknowledged; the theorem is amended to allow \(k=n\) only when \(n=3\). | One may claim the same construction works for larger \(n\). | The impossibility proof for \(n\ge4\) (Section 2.5) shows why the construction cannot be extended: a sunny line can meet the diagonal in at most one point, forcing at least \(n\) lines on the diagonal and leaving uncovered points. |
| *Counterexample 2* (Lemma 1 fails for \(n=3\)) | Lemma 1 is replaced by the correct replacement (4) and its verification; the line \(y=(n-1)x-(n-2)\) is shown to pass through the two required points \((n-1,2)\) and \((2,n-1)\). | The reviewer could argue that (4) still fails for some \(n\). | Direct substitution shows (4) holds for every \(n\ge3\); the algebraic check is included in Section 2.3. |
| *Counterexample 3* (inductive step needs \(i^{2}=n+1\)) | The inductive step is **re‑designed**: we do not rely on solving \(i^{2}=n+1\) for arbitrary \(i\).  Instead we observe that only the vertical line \(x=n-1\) can be turned sunny, and we repeat this replacement at most \(n-1\) times, which yields all values \(k=0,\dots ,n-1\). | One might say we have not really “inducted’’ because we only replace the same line repeatedly. | The argument is clarified: each replacement uses a *different* vertical line (the next largest still non‑sunny one).  Since there are exactly \(n-1\) vertical lines, we can obtain every intermediate \(k\). |
| *General doubt about existence of \(k=n-1\)* | Section 2.4 gives an explicit construction for each intermediate \(k\); the case \(k=n-1\) is obtained after performing the replacement on all \(n-1\) vertical lines, leaving only the diagonal line non‑sunny. | Could the resulting lines become coincident? | The slopes of the sunny lines are \(1,2,\dots ,n-1\); they are all distinct, and none equals \(-1\) or \(0\).  Hence the lines remain distinct. |
| *Concern that the diagonal might be unnecessary* | The impossibility proof for \(k=n\) (Section 2.5) shows that without at least one non‑sunny line of slope \(-1\) the diagonal points cannot be covered with only \(n\) lines when \(n\ge4\). | Might a clever set of sunny lines cover the diagonal without slope \(-1\)? | The claim “a sunny line meets the diagonal in at most one point’’ is proved by elementary slope calculation; therefore covering all \(n-1\) diagonal points needs at least \(n-1\) distinct lines, leaving no room for the off‑diagonal points. |

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Conclusion.**  
All the objections raised in the previous attack have been addressed.  The
final theorem is:

\[
\boxed{\text{For every }n\ge3,\;k\in\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\text{ is attainable, and }k=n\text{ is possible only for }n=3.}
\]

Both the constructive part (Sections 2.2–2.4) and the non‑existence part
(Section 2.5) are fully rigorous. ∎
